title: Tunisian Brik
subtitle: Crispy Tunisian fried pastry with egg and anchovy
excerpt: Brik is a Tunisian street food of thin pastry folded around a whole egg, anchovies, and capers, then fried until the pastry is shatteringly crisp and the egg is just set. The challenge is eating it without the yolk running. That is part of the appeal.
sourceNotes: Brik is a Tunisian specialty with roots in the Ottoman period. The pastry used is called malsouka or warqa -- a paper-thin sheet similar to filo. Brik is eaten as a street food throughout Tunisia and is particularly common during Ramadan as a starter before the fast-breaking meal.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Prepare all fillings ahead. Assemble and fry just before eating.

content.text: Filo pastry is the best substitute for the traditional Tunisian malsouka. Use one sheet per brik, folded into a triangle. Work quickly once the egg is in -- filo dries out fast and the egg needs to cook before the pastry burns.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan to 180 degrees. The oil should be deep enough to come 1cm up the sides of the brik.
Lay one filo sheet flat on the work surface. Place 2 anchovy fillets, a few capers, and a pinch of parsley in the centre.
Make a small hollow in the filling and crack 1 egg into it. Season the egg with a pinch of salt.
Fold the pastry over quickly to make a triangle, enclosing the egg. Press the edges firmly to seal.
Carefully lower into the hot oil. Fry for 2 minutes on each side until golden and crisp.
Remove and drain briefly. Serve immediately with a wedge of lemon. The yolk should still be slightly runny.

items.symptom: Egg is overcooked and yolk is hard
items.cause: Oil too hot or frying too long
items.fix: Keep the oil at 180 degrees and time exactly 2 minutes per side

items.symptom: Pastry breaks and egg leaks into the oil
items.fix: Press the edges together firmly; dampen them with a little water to help them stick
Always bring the oil up to temperature before adding the brik

content.text: Brik is sold on street corners across Tunisia, particularly in Tunis and Sfax. It is eaten as a fast lunch, a Ramadan starter, and a celebration food. The combination of crispy pastry, salty anchovy, and runny egg yolk is one of the most satisfying things in North African cooking.
